meta.notes: Market: EU mid-market and large fashion brands/retailers. The ban (ESPR Art. 25) has applied to large companies since 19 July 2026; recycling counts as destruction. Several sources were unfetchable (just-style, Otrium, Recovo, Inspectorio, Greenpeace PDF, Mammut PDF, EuroCommerce, LSA, WSJ via marketscreener) and are not cited. Founder-listed ZeroW: no public evidence found. Recovo: site disallowed by robots.txt, so not included as a competitor. Budget unknown: no evidence. Prospects: 20 companies for the primary ICP (large EU fashion brands/retailers); ASOS is UK-headquartered but sells into the EU and is included because it publishes an ESPR disclosure. Contacts only from companies' own pages (9 people at 7 companies). Several company pages were thin (Inditex, Benetton, s.Oliver, Otto, OTB), so city locations in several entries come from general knowledge and are not evidenced; their geography and size are omitted. No company-specific problem evidence (e.g. job postings) was found except ASOS and H&M.

evidence.title: Deep Dive: EU Finalises New Requirements for Unsold Consumer Products Under ESPR (Cooley)
evidence.quote: (applies from July 19, 2026) A ban on the destruction of certain unsold consumer products – currently footwear, apparel and clothing accessories (e.g. hats, ties, belts, scarves, etc.), as identified in Annex VII. This ban also prohibits the recycling of these unsold products.
evidence.statement: The ESPR destruction ban for apparel, accessories and footwear applies from 19 July 2026 and also prohibits recycling unsold products, so recycling is not a free routing outlet.

evidence.title: Discarded Products Reporting (ASOS plc)
evidence.quote: Destruction of unsold goods only occurs as a last resort where products are required to be destroyed, for example due to a legal requirement, a health & safety requirement, or in cases where products cannot be sold
evidence.statement: ASOS publishes an ESPR discarded-goods disclosure describing destruction only as a last resort.

summary.statement: Practitioner benchmarks put apparel inventory carrying cost at about 20-25% of inventory value per year.
Recovery on excess apparel is low: outlet 30-60% and B2B liquidation 20-40% of cost, and distressed apparel auctions about 1.4-2% of retail value.
One vendor claims customers cut manual labour 44%, storage 30% and disposal 18% on end-of-life handling; this is a self-reported estimate.
No public source quantified what brands spend today on preparing unsold-goods disclosures.
Most unsold stock already leaves through non-destruction channels: the Commission estimates only 4-9% of unsold textiles are destroyed.
Industry associations in Germany and Benelux say surpluses already go to outlets, charity, sales and stock buyers, with only minimal quantities discarded.
Large retailers use sample sales and third-party resellers (ASOS), discreet B2B marketplaces (smatch, Unfrosen) and direct NDA deals with resellers.
Bulk export of unsold stock to non-EU traders counts as reuse on paper and remains a cheap legal route.
In France, the 2022 AGEC ban pushed volume into donation: one network's corporate donations rose from 3 million products in 2019 to 10 million in 2023.
Disposition data typically sits in ERPs, delivery notes and recycler emails, and brands depend on waste providers to report each batch's fate.
ASOS's own disclosure says it still needs data collection to verify reseller behaviour and waste treatment routes.
The rules require five years of delivery and reception documentation, including waste-operator statements, and documented reasoning for each derogation.

Companies are preparing mainly by gathering data and amending contracts with disposal providers; third-party assurance was dropped and the mandatory template only applies from FY2028 for calendar-year companies.
Software vendors (TrusTrace, Dcycle, ReBound) already market tracking and ESPR disclosure preparation.
Unsold inventory is moving from operations to a metric sustainability, finance and compliance teams monitor.
H&M Group created a Chief Supply Chain Officer role with end-to-end responsibility for inventory flow.
A compliance adviser says the work is primarily logistical: warehouses, shops, customer services and waste providers.
No source identified who signs off on budget for disposition software specifically.

No public evidence was found on how fashion brands budget for unsold-goods compliance or reverse-logistics software; the low recovery value of distressed apparel suggests revenue share on routed goods may be small.
Brands value discretion: resellers report NDA-only relationships and brands not wanting to be on a central list; off-price platforms sell on anonymity.
Brand protection limits donation and resale of recognisable items, and repair is uneconomic for low-value garments.
Partner capacity is constrained: donation networks reject 15-20% of offers, sorters are overloaded, and EU mechanical recycling covers about 1% of the volume.
Recycling counts as destruction under the ban, so recyclers are only a valid outlet under a documented derogation.
The ban has applied to large companies since 19 July 2026, and advisers expect substantial operational and cost challenges for high-return online sellers; the sector is described as ill-prepared.
Urgency is undercut by weak enforcement: French fines cap at EUR 15,000 and the French enforcer was not yet empowered as of September 2026; penalties vary by Member State.
The German textile association calls the ban a paper tiger, and many SMEs are waiting for the full framework before acting.
The mandatory disclosure template applies only from FY2028 for calendar-year companies, and earlier delays left companies in legal limbo about format.

current_solutions.statement: Most unsold apparel already exits through outlets, sales, charity, stock buyers and third-party resellers; only 4-9% is destroyed.
Discreet B2B off-price marketplaces (smatch, Unfrosen) and NDA deals with resellers absorb excess while protecting brand image.
Donation intermediaries (Comerso, Agence du Don en Nature, broker start-ups) already handle corporate unsold goods in France.
Reporting is assembled from ERP data, delivery notes and provider emails under amended contracts, with emerging software from TrusTrace, Dcycle, ReBound and Musthad.
